_comment: The event-topic registry, as a cross-language fixture.
OWNERS: services/hub/internal/capspec/eventtopics.go (Go, the ENFORCER — mayConsume
and mayPublish read it) and apps/desktop/src/renderer/src/lib/pluginPermissions.ts
(TypeScript, the DISCLOSER — the install-consent dialog and the plugins manager).
Each side is pinned to this file by its own test, so neither can move without the
other going red: eventtopics_test.go TestEventTopicRegistryMatchesTheConsentFixture
and pluginPermissions.test.ts.
WHY IT EXISTS. The renderer used to carry a hand-copied table of the five
guarded-by-capability rows and nothing else. All the host-only rows were absent, so
a manifest declaring consumes: ["plugin.log", "sidecar.*"] rendered as an ordinary
line at severity NORMAL — plugin.log being one verbatim, unredacted line of a
sidecar's stdout/stderr, whose environment carries WKS_SETTINGS with secret plugin
settings in PLAINTEXT, and plugin.loaded the whole Manifest: install argv, the
sidecar's server command, and every declared filesystem scope. The consent dialog
was the stated justification for plugins being exempt from the registry in the first
place; a disclosure surface that under-warns is the one failure mode that matters.
THE THREE DISPOSITIONS (the reason for each row lives in eventtopics.go, which is
the enforcing copy — this file carries the SHAPE, not the argument):
guarded-by-capability  the payload is that capability's output; holding the
capability is the price of receiving the topic.
host-only              no capability returns this payload and no scoped tier or
plugin has any business with it. Trusted connections only.
open-by-decision       every tier may receive it, with the reason on the record.
CONSENT RENDERING. `severityByDisposition` is the normative mapping from a
disposition to how the dialog must render a `consumes` line that reaches it. Both
non-open dispositions are sensitive: guarded because the same reach spelled as a
capability renders sensitive, host-only because asking for host-internal state is a
fact about the plugin whether or not the bus then refuses it. Only the Go side of
this pair enforces; only the TS side renders — so `cases` are loaded by the TS test
alone, while `topics` is normative for both.
A topic in NO row is not host state (example.clock.tick, the rules engine's
command.*): a scoped user token is refused it (fail closed) and a plugin's manifest
is the only gate. It renders as an ordinary line, and that is correct.
The block registry every fixture in contracts/ must declare (cmd/brain
corpusvocab_test.go and its TypeScript twin). `topics` uses `disposition` as its
verdict field, which is what forbids the two shapes a hand-edit produces: a
guarded row with no capability behind it, and a host-only row that names one —
the second being how a topic no capability can unlock would come to look
unlockable, and the dialog would then offer the user a capability to blame.

topics.why: one classified event topic. NORMATIVE for both languages: the hub reads its copy in mayConsume/mayPublish, the renderer reads its copy to describe a manifest's `consumes` lines.
loaders: apps/desktop/src/renderer/tests/pluginPermissions.test.ts::classifies exactly the topics the fixture classifies

cases.why: how the install-consent dialog must render a manifest's `consumes` lines. TypeScript-only: the hub enforces the table and does not render it.

cases.name: the sidecar control plane, which used to render as two ordinary lines
the manifest that reads a sidecar's whole confinement map
a wildcard that spans the host-only plugin family
the capability-guarded topics still name their capability
open-by-decision and plugin-defined topics stay ordinary, so the flag still means something
